name: LevelDB
summary: An embedded ordered key-value library that combines a write log and memtable with sorted table levels, background compaction, and sequence-bounded snapshots.

features.name: Persistent ordered key-value API
features.description: The public DB interface defines a persistent ordered map from byte-string keys to values, with Put, Delete, WriteBatch, Get, iteration, and range compaction operations.
benefits: Provides a small embeddable storage boundary
Supports ordered iteration and application-defined key comparison
costs: Does not provide SQL, secondary indexes, or a built-in client-server boundary
A database is restricted to one accessing process

features.name: Log, memtable, and leveled sorted tables
features.description: Recent updates are appended to a log and represented in a memtable; the memtable is converted to sorted tables, which are organized into levels with non-overlapping ranges outside level zero.
benefits: Turns sequential updates into sorted immutable files
Separates foreground update state from durable table organization
costs: Memory buffers and immutable files add space and recovery work

features.name: Background leveled compaction
features.description: When level size thresholds are exceeded, background compaction merges a level's files with overlapping files in the next level, discarding overwritten values and obsolete deletion markers when safe.
benefits: Reduces the number of files and read merging work
Bulk merges gradually move updates toward larger levels
costs: Compaction consumes I/O and CPU and can create latency pressure

features.name: Sequence-bounded snapshots and log recovery
features.description: The API exposes immutable snapshots of the current database state; the implementation assigns sequence numbers to batches and recovery replays log records into a memtable before restoring the serving state.
benefits: Provides stable read boundaries while later writes continue
Makes restart reconstruction explicit through log and manifest state
costs: Long-lived snapshots retain versions and delay cleanup
Recovery time grows with the unflushed log

mathematical_views.question: How does a logical ordered map refine into a write log, memtable, sorted-table levels, and compaction generations?
assumptions: Updates are compared at explicit sequence boundaries
Flush and compaction preserve the visible key-value map
File count, I/O, and memory are modeled as costs rather than logical state

mathematical_views.question: Which version of each key is visible to an iterator associated with a snapshot sequence?
assumptions: Write batches receive monotonically increasing sequence numbers
A snapshot fixes a read boundary while later writes remain outside it
Compaction preserves versions required by live snapshots

mathematical_views.question: Which log, manifest, and sorted-table states reconstruct a valid logical database after reopening?
assumptions: Log records are replayed in generation order
The model distinguishes acknowledged writes from the configured sync boundary

costs: Limited data model and no built-in network service

benefits: Sequential writes with sorted persistent representation
costs: Read and space amplification across levels
Compaction resource pressure and bursty latency

benefits: Stable reads and deterministic restart path
costs: Pinned versions and recovery-time dependence on log state
